title: DeCoRL: Decomposed Consistency Reinforcement Learning for Multi-Image Composition
claim: Baselines break object identity and attributes when composing many references; ours preserves every referenced object consistently.
layout: 4 rows: reference strip then outputs, two examples, red boxes mark errors
description: Two stacked qualitative examples, each with six reference images across the top row (Picture 1–6) and a row of six generated results below. The first example uses a banana bunch, a milkshake glass, a coffee cup, tulips, a yellow lamp and a white chair, composed into a room scene. The second uses a woman in a beanie, a patterned cap, beige flats, a pink handbag, a vintage camera and a brown suitcase, composed into a train-station scene. Output columns are labeled Qwen-Image-Edit-MICo, Qwen-Image-Edit-UniPic3.0, FLUX.2-dev, Seedream4.0 (2K), Nano-Banana-Pro and Ours (bold, rightmost). Red rectangles on baseline outputs mark objects with the wrong shape, color or identity. The eye goes to the red boxes first, and the last column has none.
caption: Qualitative comparisons on two challenging MICo examples, each involving six reference images. Compared with open-source and proprietary baselines, our method better preserves the identities and visual attributes of multiple referenced objects in the composed image. The red boxes highlight objects with inconsistent appearances.
abstract: Multi-image composition (MICo) is a critical yet challenging capability for large-scale image editing models, where consistency degrades rapidly as the number of reference images increases. While supervised fine-tuning (SFT) can equip models with basic MICo ability, it provides only implicit supervision on the composed image and often fails to learn reliable object-level correspondence across multiple references. We propose DeCoRL, a reinforcement-learning (RL) framework that improves MICo consistency by decomposing holistic MICo consistency into object-level consistency. DeCoRL first establishes instruction-relevant object correspondences across reference images and localizes the corresponding regions in the generated image. It then uses a VLM-based reward model trained on single-object consistency annotations to produce fine-grained, object-wise feedback, which is aggregated into a multi-object consistency reward to guide RL post-training. We further introduce DeCo-Bench, a benchmark covering compositions from 2 to 6 reference images. Experiments on DeCo-Bench and the public MICo-Bench demonstrate consistent improvements in MICo consistency.
